clips.text: Welcome to today's walk through an Italian market. You already met numbers up to twenty in the foundations course, and today they go to work. In the next ten minutes you will buy fruit by the kilo, ask prices, and order politely, all by recombining a handful of blocks.
First, a quick recap. One to ten in Italian. You know these cold, and everything today is priced and weighed with them. Listen once to lock them in.
Uno, due, tre, quattro, cinque, sei, sette, otto, nove, dieci.
Now eleven to twenty. They stack onto ten the way English stacks teens. Notice seventeen and nineteen keep their full shape. Listen, because in two minutes these become prices.
Undici, dodici, tredici, quattordici, quindici, sedici, diciassette, diciotto, diciannove, venti.
Quick check before we move on. Seventeen. You heard it buried in the list. Say it in your head right now. Ten seconds, then listen to confirm.
Diciassette.

At an Italian market you buy quantities, not pieces. Two tiny words do the heavy lifting: a feminine word pairs with one of them, a masculine word with the other. Listen to how a kilo of apples is ordered.
Un chilo di mele.
Next block: short for one hundred grams. Cold cuts and cheese sell by it. A hundred grams of ham. Listen to the pattern with apples, then ham.
Un etto di prosciutto.
Una fetta di formaggio.

Now prices. How much does it cost, for one thing. Think. You are at the stall with one melon in your hand. Build the question yourself, then take ten seconds and say it in your head. Then listen to the reveal.
Quanto costa un melone?
Many things change exactly one word: it gains an n, meaning they cost. Think. A pile of peaches catches your eye. Ask the vendor their price, then listen.
Quanto costano le pesche?
Answers come back as numbers you already own. Listen and count with the vendor: three euros, that is four euros, five euros and fifty cents.
Tre euro.
Sono quattro euro.
Cinque euro e cinquanta.
Now the politest verb in the market: I would like, softer than I want. Please opens every request, and thanks closes it. Listen to a full request.
Due etti di prosciutto, per favore.
Markets run on greetings: good morning, many thanks, goodbye, until tomorrow. Listen to each.
Buongiorno, grazie mille!
Arrivederci, a domani!
Time to put it together. A customer, Elena, at a fruit stall. She greets, the vendor answers, she orders a kilo of apples, and asks the price of the grapes. Listen to the whole exchange.
Buongiorno! Vorrei un chilo di mele, per favore.
Buongiorno! Mi dica pure.
Quanto costano le pesche?
Grazie mille, arrivederci!

Now you are Elena. The vendor greets you. You want three apples. Build the polite request, then the grapes catch your eye: one kilo, so the singular question. Ten seconds for both lines, in your head, then listen.
Vorrei tre mele, per favore.
Quanto costa un chilo di uva?

One more stall, cheese this time, and the vendor answers back. Two new half-blocks: a price sentence that needs no verb phrase of its own, and a short word that takes the feminine thing, while masculine things take another form. Listen to the whole exchange: question, price, deal.
Quanto costa una fetta di formaggio?
Costa due euro.
La prendo, grazie.
Final challenge, and nobody taught you this one. You are back at the fruit stall. One melon, masculine. Ask its price, singular, then take it, masculine. Twelve seconds, in your head, then listen.
Quanto costa un melone?
He names the price. Now close the deal. The melon is masculine, so the short word is the masculine one. Listen.
Lo prendo, grazie.
One more review, mixing every block. Pears are feminine plural, and you want one kilo, so the masculine quantity word is right. A polite request, twelve seconds, in your head, then listen.
Vorrei un chilo di pere, per favore.

And that is the market. Gender picks the little word for a and one. Kilo and hundred grams weigh it. One thing or many things changes the price verb. Please and thank you wrap every request in politeness, and the verb for taking closes the deal. A handful of blocks, and you derived every sentence today, including ones nobody taught you.
